blocks.text: The sea-monsters and Leviathan in verses 13–14 draw on both recognizable animal traits and larger mythopoetic, cosmic imagery. Leviathan therefore need not be treated as a narrowly identifiable ordinary animal; the image is deliberately larger than a field-guide description. The precise referent remains disputed.

The prayer speaks throughout as a wounded community: “us,” “thy congregation,” and “thy poor.” Its grief over a ruined sanctuary belongs alongside communal psalms that preserve the memory of sanctuary destruction and Babylonian exile. That wider setting helps explain why the psalm joins anguish over devastation with an urgent appeal for God to remember the covenant and defend his name, while the specific historical setting of this psalm remains disputed.
